title: Singly linked list: insertEnd, reverseList, display
statement:
Anitha stores the song numbers of her playlist in a singly linked list. The program has three functions: insertEnd adds a new song at the end of the list, reverseList reverses the order of the songs in the list by changing the links between the nodes and returns the new first node, and display prints the song numbers of the list from the first node to the last node, separated by single spaces, without any extra space at the end.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers (song numbers in the order added).
Output Format: Line 1: "Original: " + numbers separated by spaces. Line 2: "Reversed: " + numbers after reversing.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 50; 1 <= song number <= 10000
easy: Build a linked list by adding each song at the end, print it, reverse the links in place, and print it again.
logic: insertEnd walks to the last node (while temp->next != NULL) and attaches the new node; an empty list returns the new node as head.
reverseList uses three pointers (prev, curr, nextNode): flip each link and finally return prev (the old last node).
display prints each number and a space only when a next node exists - no trailing space.
algorithm: struct Node { int data; Node* next; };
insertEnd(head, value): create node; if head == NULL return it; walk to the end; attach; return head.
reverseList(head): prev = NULL; curr = head; while curr: save next, curr->next = prev, prev = curr, curr = next; return prev.
display(head): print data; if next != NULL print a space; repeat until NULL; then endl.
main: read n values building the list, print Original, reverse, print Reversed.
mistakes: Reversing by copying values instead of changing the links (the task requires link reversal).
Forgetting to return prev from reverseList - the head would still point to the (now) last node.
Printing a trailing space after the last number - exact-output platforms reject it.

title: Circular queue with array (enqueue / dequeue / show)
statement:
Dhanush designs the buffer of a printer, which can hold only a fixed number of print jobs. The buffer is a circular queue implemented with an array, so the space freed at the front of the array is reused by the new jobs added at the rear. The function process takes a type and a value. When the type is 1, it adds the job number given in value at the rear, and prints "Enqueued " followed by the job number, or prints "Queue Full" if the buffer has no free space. When the type is 2, it removes the job at the front, and prints "Dequeued " followed by the job number, or prints "Queue Empty" if the buffer has no job. The function show prints the jobs in the buffer from the front to the rear.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: capacity c and number of operations n. Next n lines: type (1 or 2) and value (0 for type 2, ignored).
Output Format: One message per operation. Last line: "Queue:" followed by " job" for each job front-to-rear, or "Queue: Empty".
Constraints: 1 <= c <= 10; 1 <= n <= 30; 1 <= value <= 1000 for type 1
easy: A fixed-size circular buffer: keep front, rear and count; the modulo operator wraps the indexes around the end of the array.
logic: Enqueue when count < capacity: rear = (rear + 1) % capacity; store; count++; print Enqueued.
Dequeue when count > 0: print arr[front]; front = (front + 1) % capacity; count--.
count (not front/rear comparison) decides Full and Empty - that is the cleanest correct rule.
show prints count elements starting at front, each at (front + i) % capacity.
algorithm: class CircularQueue with arr[100], capacity, front = 0, rear = -1, count = 0.
process(1, v): if count == capacity print "Queue Full"; else place at ++rear mod capacity.
process(2, 0): if count == 0 print "Queue Empty"; else print arr[front] as Dequeued and advance front.
show(): if count == 0 print "Queue: Empty"; else "Queue:" then loop i = 0..count-1 printing " " << arr[(front + i) % capacity].
mistakes: Using rear == capacity - 1 as the full condition (breaks after wraps); use count == capacity.
Forgetting % capacity on BOTH enqueue and dequeue.
Wrong show format: the label is "Queue:" with a space before EVERY job, and "Queue: Empty" when count is 0.
note: Hidden test 4/10 exercises two wraps - a linear (non-circular) queue fails it.

title: Circular linked list: insertEnd and walking n steps
statement:
Chitra organises a game in which players sit around a round table. The player numbers are stored in a circular linked list, where the last node points back to the first node. The function insertEnd adds a new player after the last player, and keeps the list circular. The function valueAfterSteps starts from the first player, moves forward the given number of steps around the table, and returns the player number reached. The number of steps can be larger than the number of players, so the walk can go around the table more than once. Moving 0 steps returns the first player.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers (player numbers in sitting order). Line 3: integer steps.
Output Format: "Value After Steps: " + player number reached.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 50; 1 <= player number <= 10000; 0 <= steps <= 200
easy: Build a circular list (last node points back to the first), then walk exactly `steps` links forward from the head and report the value found there.
logic: insertEnd: for an empty list the new node points to ITSELF; otherwise walk while temp->next != head, attach the new node, and point the new node back to head.
valueAfterSteps simply does temp = temp->next exactly `steps` times - the circularity handles the wrapping automatically.
No modulo is needed on the steps: moving around the ring many times is fine.
algorithm: insertEnd(head, value): newNode->data = value; if head == NULL { newNode->next = newNode; return newNode; } walk while temp->next != head; temp->next = newNode; newNode->next = head; return head.
valueAfterSteps(head, steps): temp = head; repeat steps times temp = temp->next; return temp->data.
main: read n, build list, read steps, print "Value After Steps: " + result.
mistakes: Building a LINEAR list (last node pointing to NULL) instead of circular.
Walking steps - 1 times instead of steps (0 steps must return the FIRST player).
Stopping the insertion walk with temp->next != NULL - in a circular list it never becomes NULL, causing an infinite loop.
note: Sample 4 players + 5 steps = index 1 (wrap once): value 6.

title: Postfix expression evaluation with a stack
statement:
Eswari builds a calculator for her students that evaluates expressions written in postfix form. In a postfix expression, the operator comes after its two operands. For example, 23+ means 2 + 3, and 93- means 9 - 3. Every operand is a single digit from 0 to 9, and the operators are +, -, *, and /. The division is an integer division. The function evaluate uses a stack to evaluate the expression and returns the result.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: One line: string expr (valid postfix, digits 0-9 and + - * /, no division by zero).
Output Format: "Result: " + integer value.
Constraints: 1 <= length of expr <= 49
easy: Scan the expression left to right: digits go on the stack; every operator pops two values, computes, and pushes the answer back. The final stack top is the result.
logic: Digit character c -> push c - '0' (converts '7' to 7).
Operator -> pop b FIRST, then pop a (order matters for - and /).
Compute a op b with integer division for / and push the result.
After the scan, the answer is stack[top].
algorithm: int stack[50]; int top = -1;
For each char: if digit, stack[++top] = c - '0'.
Else: b = stack[top--]; a = stack[top--]; result = a op b; stack[++top] = result.
Return stack[top]. main prints "Result: " + evaluate(expr).
mistakes: Popping a before b (then a - b / a / b are computed backwards - sample 92- would give -6 instead of 6).
Using float division: the task requires integer division (82/ = 4, not 4.0).
Forgetting c - '0' when pushing - pushing the ASCII value 50 instead of 2.

title: Doubly linked list: insertFront and two-way printing
statement:
Bhuvan builds a "recent files" list for a text editor using a doubly linked list. Every file number that is opened is added at the front of the list, so the newest file is always the first node. The program keeps a pointer to the first node and a pointer to the last node of the list. The function insertFront adds a new file at the front, the function printForward prints the file numbers from the first node to the last node, and the function printBackward prints the file numbers from the last node to the first node by following the previous links.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers (file numbers in the order opened).
Output Format: Line 1: "Forward:" + numbers (each preceded by a space). Line 2: "Backward:" + numbers reversed.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 50; 1 <= file number <= 10000
easy: Each new file becomes the new first node of a doubly linked list; forward printing follows next, backward printing follows prev from the tail.
logic: insertFront: newNode->next = old head; if the list was empty, tail = newNode; else head->prev = newNode; then head = newNode.
printForward walks head -> next until NULL.
printBackward walks tail -> prev until NULL.
Both use the " " before each value format.
algorithm: void insertFront(Node*& head, Node*& tail, int value): create node; node->prev = NULL; node->next = head; if head == NULL tail = node; else head->prev = node; head = node.
printForward(Node* head): "Forward:" loop with " " << data via next.
printBackward(Node* tail): "Backward:" loop with " " << data via prev.
main: read n values, insert each at front, print both directions.
mistakes: Forgetting to update tail when the FIRST node is inserted - backward printing would crash or print wrong order.
Forgetting head->prev = newNode - the backward chain would break.
Passing head/tail by value - the caller never sees the change; they must be references (Node*&).

title: Complete binary tree traversals from array indices
statement:
Dr. Anita maintains the reporting hierarchy of a college department as a complete binary tree. The employee IDs are stored level by level in an array, so the node at index i has its left child at index 2i + 1 and its right child at index 2i + 2, provided those indices are less than the number of nodes. Write a program that reads the array and prints the preorder (root, left, right), inorder (left, root, right), and postorder (left, right, root) traversals of the tree, using recursion on the array indices.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers (node values level by level, root at index 0).
Output Format: "Preorder: ", "Inorder: ", "Postorder: " lines with values separated by spaces.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 100; 1 <= node values <= 1000
easy: The tree lives inside a plain array: children of index i sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2. Three recursive functions print the three traversals.
logic: A recursive visit(i) first checks i >= n (outside the tree) and returns.
Preorder: print a[i], then recurse left, then right.
Inorder: left, print a[i], right. Postorder: left, right, print a[i].
The QB's reference solution uses C (stdio) - the C++17 version below has identical logic with cin/cout.
algorithm: void preorder(int i): if (i >= n) return; visit a[i]; preorder(2i+1); preorder(2i+2).
void inorder(int i): if (i >= n) return; inorder(2i+1); visit a[i]; inorder(2i+2).
void postorder(int i): if (i >= n) return; postorder(2i+1); postorder(2i+2); visit a[i].
Collect values then print each line as "Label:" + " value" for every collected value.
mistakes: Forgetting the i >= n base case - recursion runs off the end of the array.
Mixing up inorder (root in the MIDDLE) and preorder (root FIRST).
Printing the label with a missing colon or double space before values - the format is exactly "Preorder: 15 10 5 20".
note: Both the original C version and the C++ conversion were compiled and passed all 6 cases.

title: Binary min-heap built by repeated insertion
statement:
Tarun is designing a help desk where every support ticket carries a priority number, and a smaller number means a more urgent ticket. The tickets are kept in a binary min-heap stored in an array, so that the most urgent ticket is always at index 0. Write a program that inserts the given priorities into an initially empty min-heap one by one. Each new value is placed at the end of the array and then moved up: while its parent is larger, swap it with the parent. The parent of the element at index i is at index (i - 1) / 2 using integer division. Print the array after all insertions.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers (priorities in arrival order).
Output Format: "Min-Heap:" followed by the heap array separated by spaces.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 100; 1 <= priorities <= 1000
easy: Insert every number at the end of an array, then bubble it UP while its parent is bigger - the result is a min-heap (smallest on top).
logic: h[size] = x; i = size; size++ - place the new value at the end.
While i > 0 and h[(i-1)/2] > h[i]: swap with the parent and set i = parent.
Repeat for every incoming value, then print the whole array.
algorithm: Read n; size = 0.
For each x: h[size] = x; i = size; size++;
Print "Min-Heap:" then " h[i]" for i = 0..size-1.
mistakes: Swapping while the parent is SMALLER (that builds a max-heap).
Computing the parent index as i/2 - it is (i - 1) / 2.
Printing a trailing space - the format is "Min-Heap: 3 9 7 12" with the colon-space-space pattern exactly as the QB samples show.
note: Sample 12 7 3 9 ends as 3 9 7 12 - trace it by hand once, it teaches the whole algorithm.

title: Postfix expression to fully parenthesised infix (expression tree)
statement:
Lavanya is teaching a compiler design lab and wants to show her students how a postfix expression turns into an expression tree. In an expression tree, every leaf holds an operand and every internal node holds an operator whose left and right children are its two operands. Write a program that reads a postfix expression and builds its expression tree using a stack of tree nodes: push a new node for every operand, and for every operator create a node, make the top of the stack its right child, the next one its left child, and push it back. Finally, print the expression in infix form by an inorder traversal, wrapping every operator node and its two operands in a pair of parentheses. A single operand is printed without parentheses.
Note: the QB reference solution uses malloc(); the C++17 version below uses new.
Input Format: One line: string s (postfix, lowercase operands, operators + - * /, no spaces).
Output Format: "Infix Expression: " + fully parenthesised infix.
Constraints: 1 <= length of s <= 50
easy: Build a tree from the postfix string using a node stack, then walk it inorder and wrap every operator in brackets.
logic: Operand char -> create a leaf node and push it.
Operator char -> pop RIGHT child first, then LEFT child, attach both, push the operator node.
Inorder print: if leaf, print the character; else print (, left, operator, right, ).
algorithm: struct Node { char data; Node *left, *right; }; newNode(c) allocates and clears.
Stack of Node* with top = -1.
For each char c: node = newNode(c); if (c is an operator) { node->right = pop; node->left = pop; } push node.
printInfix(root): leaf -> print data; else '(' + left + data + right + ')'.
Print "Infix Expression: " then the traversal then endl.
mistakes: Popping LEFT before RIGHT - for non-commutative operators (-, /) the tree would be mirrored (x-y would print (y-x)).
Wrapping single operands in brackets - a leaf prints WITHOUT parentheses.
Forgetting the "Infix Expression: " label prefix.

title: BST search with depth of the found key
statement:
Suresh organises the digital catalogue of a library in a binary search tree of book IDs. Each book ID is inserted in the order it was received: an ID smaller than the current node goes to the left subtree, and an ID larger than the current node goes to the right subtree. All book IDs in the catalogue are different. Write a program that builds the binary search tree from the given IDs and then searches for a given key starting from the root. The depth of a node is the number of edges on the path from the root to that node, so the root has depth 0. If the key is in the tree, print its depth, otherwise report that it was not found.
Note: the QB reference solution uses malloc(); the C++17 version below uses new.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: n integers (IDs in insertion order). Line 3: integer key.
Output Format: "Found at depth <d>" or "Not Found".
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 100; 1 <= IDs, key <= 1000; all IDs distinct
easy: Insert every ID into a BST, then walk down comparing with the key; count how many edges you pass - that is the depth.
logic: insert(root, x): empty spot -> create node; x < data -> go left; else go right (recursively).
Search: while curr != NULL and curr->data != key: move left/right and depth++.
If curr becomes NULL the key is missing -> "Not Found".
algorithm: Node* insert(Node* root, int x): if root == NULL return new node(x); if (x < root->data) root->left = insert(root->left, x); else root->right = insert(root->right, x); return root.
Read n, insert all IDs.
curr = root; depth = 0; while (curr && curr->data != key) { curr = key < curr->data ? curr->left : curr->right; depth++; }
Print "Found at depth " + depth or "Not Found".
mistakes: Starting depth at 1 - the root is depth 0.
Comparing with >= (duplicates are impossible here, but equal keys must STOP the search).
Counting depth during INSERT instead of during the explicit search walk (works only if done carefully - the clean way is the search loop).
note: Chained insertion 10 20 30 40 50 60 makes a right-leaning chain: key 60 is at depth 5.
